newsitem.title: CYPRUS: Britain hopeful talks can start in Cyprus-envoy.
newsitem.headline: Britain hopeful talks can start in Cyprus-envoy.

text.p: Britain expressed hope on Wednesday that Greek and Turkish Cypriots could start direct negotations by June to try to resolve the long-standing division of the island.
Leaders of the two communities, divided since a Turkish invasion of the northern third of the island in 1974, have not met since October 1994.

Sir David Hannay, Britain's special envoy for Cyprus, started contacts on the island on Wednesday as the United Nations pushed to get direct negotiations under way after proximity talks, which began on Monday.
Hannay said it was up to the U.N. secretary-general, Kofi Annan, to decide when to conclude the preparatory stage and call the two sides to direct talks.

"Our hope remains that he (the Secretary-General) will convene face-to-face negotiations before the end of the first half of 1997," Hannay told reporters after meeting Cypriot President Glafcos Clerides.
Later in the afternoon Hannay is scheduled to meet Turkish Cypriot leader Rauf Denktash across the U.N.-controlled "green line" snaking through the divided capital in north Nicosia.
The British official has dismissed suggestions that he will submit a blueprint solution, but has refused to be specific on the range of issues he will discuss.
Cyprus has been divided since Turkey invaded in 1974 in response to a short-lived Greek Cypriot coup engineered by the military ruling in Greece at the time.
Britain, along with Greece and Turkey, is a guarantor power of Cyprus, a former British colony which became independent in 1960.

Turkish Cypriots now live in the north, where they proclaimed a state recognised only by Ankara in 1983. The Greek Cypriot administration in the south is internationally recognised as the legitimate government of Cyprus.
United Nations attempts to reunite the island under a federal umbrella in accordance with high-level agreements reached between the two sides in 1977 and 1979 have stalled.
Hannay refused to elaborate on his two-hour meeting with Clerides.

"It really isn't conducive to the development of a process which is very sensitive on all sides and which we hope, all of us hope, is going to be more sucessful than previous attempts to negotiate a solution," he said.
